about.intro: I grew up in Fernhollow and studied commerce at Fernhollow College of Commerce. After graduating, a friend and I started Bindwell, a binding and photocopy kiosk for students' theses and project reports. It handled 2,400 jobs in 22 months and then I closed it, because every overnight rush job lost money. In 2021 I joined Pinewick Paper & Print in Larchmont Falls on the order desk, moved to the regional strategy and operations team in 2023 and led operations for the first Print Desk town launch. I started the PGP at Ravenmoor Institute of Management in 2025 to step into a founder's office job, and spent the summer interning at Tallowfield Freight.
about.now: Writing The Back Office Bulletin on Sundays, dropping blitz games at a Ravenmoor café on Saturdays and out on the ridge road by 5 am when I manage it.

threadly-operating-cadence.context: Tallowfield Freight is a Larchmont Falls courier and haulage firm with a dispatch hub, two depots and a growing fleet. By 2026 six teams reported to the founder, and the Monday meeting was the one place they all sat together.
threadly-operating-cadence.problem: Every team reported in its own format. The meeting ran close to two and a half hours, nothing was recorded, and only 38% of Monday's commitments had been delivered a week later.
what_i_did: Observed three meetings and timed every topic, noting which ones ended in a decision. 61% of the clock went on settling what the figures meant.
Agreed 12 common metrics with the six leads, then wired a Looker Studio dashboard to the existing Sheets and dispatch exports.
Swapped the whiteboard tour for a single Notion page per team: three figures, what moved, and what they need from the founder.
Fixed the agenda at 60 minutes and logged every action in Slack with a named owner and a due date.
Ran the Q3 OKR round: wrote the company objectives alongside the founder, then refined key results with each lead until every one had one owner.

decisions.choice: Settle the numbers before the meeting
decisions.why: Most of the clock went on disputing definitions. With one dashboard as the source, the discussion could open on decisions.

decisions.choice: One page per team, sent the evening before
decisions.why: The founder read the updates on Sunday night anyway, so taking the reading out of the room freed the most time.

decisions.choice: Three company objectives, not one per team
decisions.why: Team OKRs written alone had overlapped. Three shared objectives made the leads agree who owned what.

results.note: average of the last 4 weeks of the internship
over 8 weeks, counted in the Slack action log

threadly-operating-cadence.learned: Two weeks went on the dashboard; persuading six leads to share one definition of 'delivered on time' took three more. The rhythm only held once the founder stopped taking verbal updates in the room.
threadly-operating-cadence.next: Give the depots a monthly review of their own, since their figures shift too slowly for a weekly slot.
threadly-operating-cadence.my_role: Founder's Office Intern, owned the review rhythm and the OKR cycle

thistledown-launch.context: In 2023 Pinewick's regional manager, Gordie Pruitt, wanted to know whether small shops, schools and clinics outside Larchmont Falls would buy standing orders of paper and printing from a Pinewick Print Desk instead of the cheap online stationers they already used. Thistledown, a river town where Pinewick kept a small depot, was the first test.
thistledown-launch.problem: There was no playbook. Nobody knew which districts to start in, how many route reps we needed, or why accounts that signed up would keep reordering. Marla Finch was sure it was a sales problem; Dennis Hale was sure it was a rounding problem.
what_i_did: Scored 14 market districts in Thistledown on small-business density and trade mix, and chose four to open first: Mill Street, Tanner's Row, Canal Road and Hobbs Lane.
Hired and trained a route team of seven with the town manager and Priya Raman in HR, and set daily visit targets by district.

Onboarded accounts through one shared sheet and a WhatsApp group per district, and repaired the three points where credit approval kept stalling, after Dennis agreed a single rounding rule for invoices.
Phoned 110 accounts that skipped their first reorder and sorted the reasons into categories.
Wrote the launch playbook from the Thistledown data, which the team used for Ashgrove.

decisions.why: They reorder on a calendar and their bills were larger than a corner shop's, so a reliable delivery slot and one monthly invoice mattered more to them than the lowest price per ream.

decisions.choice: A day-7 visit for every new account
decisions.why: Accounts that lapsed nearly always hit trouble in week one: a delivery left at the wrong door or an invoice they could not decode. A day-7 visit fixed that before they drifted back to their old supplier.

results.note: up from 47% during the launch's first month
vs 16 for Thistledown, using the playbook

thistledown-launch.learned: Whether an account stayed was settled in its first week. Those whose first delivery arrived complete, with an invoice they could read, mostly stayed; the rest mostly left. Tilly Brandt, who answers the front desk phone, had said as much a month before my numbers did.
thistledown-launch.next: Test whether a text message with the delivery photo and invoice could replace the day-7 visit in towns where route teams are expensive.
thistledown-launch.my_role: Strategy & Ops Associate, led launch operations

second-sem.context: Final-year students at Fernhollow College of Commerce and two other campuses had to print and bind a thesis, and the campus copy shop took a week. Most students started three days before the deadline and wanted it overnight.
second-sem.problem: Printing and binding was cheap to do when students planned ahead. The open question was whether the kiosk could survive once most jobs arrived as overnight rushes.
what_i_did: Ran a kiosk at the library gate with two second-hand binding machines bought from a closing print shop, and priced walk-in jobs at ₹150–400 depending on pages.
Took jobs by WhatsApp and a booking sheet, with every job tracked in Google Sheets.
Tracked contribution margin per job every month, split by walk-in and overnight rush.
When exams went online in 2020, thesis volumes dropped but the rush jobs stayed. A part-time night-shift hire for half a year only added to the cost.
Closed in June 2021 after paying every helper and supplier, selling the machines and writing up our figures in a public post-mortem.

decisions.choice: Keep walk-in prices and charge for rush
decisions.why: Walk-in jobs made ₹46 each; rush jobs lost money. A ₹120 rush fee cut overnight jobs by half.
All the growth was in overnight rush jobs, and each lost ₹27 once paper waste, overtime and reprints were counted. Fresh funding would only have lost money faster.

results.note: after paper waste, overtime and 9% reprints

second-sem.learned: I should have split margin by job type in month one. For nearly twelve months we cheered rising volume that came entirely from the job type that lost money.
second-sem.next: Starting over, I would build a planned-orders business: one kiosk per campus, booking slots and a fixed rush fee from the first day.
second-sem.my_role: Co-founder, ran purchasing, operations and finance

activation-tracker.context: I spent 2021 to 2023 as an Operations Associate on Pinewick's order desk in Larchmont Falls, handling small-business accounts between sales, finance and the warehouse.
activation-tracker.problem: Order status for small-business accounts sat in four spreadsheets, one of them Dennis Hale's, and in Slack threads. When an order stalled, no one could say whose move it was.
what_i_did: Replaced the four spreadsheets with a single Airtable base, once Dennis and I had settled which column stays his.
Connected Zapier to Slack so a stalled order raised an alert naming its owner and the next step.
Built it solo over five weeks, with two team leads and an hour a week of Wendell Odom's time on warehouse statuses.

results.note: people on the order desk, in sales and in the warehouse
taken up by 3 more pods and still running 2 years on

decisions.choice: One tracker instead of four spreadsheets
decisions.why: Order status lived in four places. In one Airtable tracker, every order had one row and one status.

decisions.choice: Slack alerts that name an owner for each stalled order
decisions.why: Zapier posted a Slack alert whenever an order stalled, naming the person who had to move it next.

activation-tracker.learned: What shifted the number was naming an owner and a next move for every stalled order: median dispatch time in my pod dropped from 5.4 to 3.2 days. Meetings now get the same treatment, with each decision recorded alongside who owns it and by when.

market-khata.context: Small stationery shops in Ferrywick reorder from wholesalers by phone and from memory, and lose sales when a best-seller runs out. We took this on for the Ravenmoor Institute of Management venture course in 2025.
market-khata.problem: Could a shop owner get a timely reorder prompt on the phone she already uses, without changing how she buys from her wholesaler?
what_i_did: Ran the four-person team across eight weeks.
Interviewed 26 shop owners at Ferrywick Wholesale Market.
Made a clickable Figma and Glide prototype: a reminder that lands on WhatsApp with a one-tap order link.
Piloted the prototype with six shops for three weeks.
Presented it on demo day for the venture course.

results.note: Ravenmoor Institute of Management venture course

decisions.choice: Reminders on WhatsApp, with an order link
decisions.why: Shop owners already take orders and payments on WhatsApp. The prototype sends the reminder there, so the reorder is one tap.

decisions.choice: Put the prototype in front of shops before demo day
decisions.why: Six shops used it for three weeks, which let the pitch show actual behaviour instead of a slide of good intentions.

market-khata.learned: Three weeks of real use by six shops gave the pitch something concrete. We placed second among 22 teams.

cloud-kitchen-pnl.context: Inkwell Express, a Ravenmoor stationery delivery brand, ran seven delivery zones but reported one company-wide profit figure. Our team of three took it on as a six-week live project for Ravenmoor Institute of Management.
cloud-kitchen-pnl.problem: Looking only at the whole company's profit, the founder had no way to tell which zones paid their way.
what_i_did: Modelled profit for all seven zones from order data, using Google Sheets with a Looker Studio view on top.
Spotted two zones that lost money per order once courier fees and free-delivery codes were charged against them.
Presented the zone figures to the founder.

results.note: the following month, once the founder shut one zone and trimmed free-delivery codes in another

decisions.choice: Profit worked out zone by zone
decisions.why: The whole-company figure hid the spread. Cutting order data by zone showed who earned their keep.

decisions.choice: Count courier fees and free-delivery codes on every order
decisions.why: Courier fees and codes are billed per order, and they are what sent two of the seven zones under water.

cloud-kitchen-pnl.learned: With figures cut by zone the call was easy: the founder shut one zone and trimmed codes in another. It echoes Bindwell: watch margin by channel from day one.

visual.title: Contribution per order, by zone
visual.note: Illustrative shape, not drawn to scale: 7 zones, 2 under zero after courier fees and free-delivery codes.

monday-review.context: The Back Office Bulletin is a fortnightly newsletter about the quiet tools that keep small companies going. It began in August 2025 and gets written on Sundays.
monday-review.problem: I wanted to understand how small companies really stay organised, so every issue rests on a conversation with someone who does that work: an accountant, a receptionist, a warehouse foreman or a founder.
what_i_did: Launched it in August 2025, midway through the PGP.
Built the issues around interviews: 15 so far, including a front-desk lead who schedules a 140-person office from one sticky note.
Wrote on Sundays about the tool, who owns it and what breaks.
Sent each issue out on a two-week cycle, with research notes filed in Notion.
Published 20 issues so far.

decisions.why: Each issue follows how a real person runs a real tool, so it describes the actual spreadsheet and the actual handover.

decisions.choice: Every two weeks, written on Sundays
decisions.why: Issues go out fortnightly and get written on Sundays, so the PGP workload is not disturbed.

monday-review.learned: A fixed publishing schedule is a rhythm in itself. It has produced 20 issues for 1,400 subscribers at a 52% open rate, and the most forwarded one covered a receptionist's call log.
